# Krate

> Krate is an open-source app runtime and AI app maker, built in Rust on Wasmtime. Describe an app and Krate Studio makes it; send it as one .krate file or a link, the way you send a picture. A link opens the app in any modern browser, phones included, with nothing to install and no account. With the Krate runtime, the same file runs natively on macOS, Windows and Linux, with no browser or WebView inside, so there is no separate package, build or signature for each operating system. Apps are small, from 37 KB, start with no access to files or the network, and ask before they touch anything. Not to be confused with Rust crates (crates.io), krate.com or KrateSoft.

Krate makes apps you send like pictures: one small .krate file that opens from a link in any browser, phones included, with nothing to install, and runs natively on macOS, Windows and Linux.

## Facts

- Current release: Krate 0.5.4 (2026-09-30).
- Runtimes: macOS (Apple silicon, Intel), Windows (x64, ARM64), Linux (x86_64, arm64).
- What the recipient installs: Nothing, to open a link: the app runs in any modern browser, phones included, with no account. To run apps natively, the recipient installs the Krate runtime once for macOS, Windows or Linux, and every .krate opens from its file after that.
- Sandbox: Every app starts with no access to files or the network. Before it opens, the person sees exactly what it asks for and decides; hosts it did not declare stay unreachable, and each app keeps its own storage. Grant only what the task needs.
- Licences: the Krate runtime, format and CLI are free and open source (MIT OR Apache-2.0). Studio has separate licensing (Business Source License 1.1); see the repository license details.
- Studio: Krate Studio makes and changes apps with AI: describe the app in plain words and it writes, checks and packs it, then keep changing it by asking. Studio runs on macOS, Windows and Linux and in the browser at krate.tech/app/, and works with Claude, Codex, Grok or Gemini. Developers can also build with the krate command line and the Rust SDK.
- Bundles: A .krate bundle contains a WebAssembly component and manifest, and can also carry source, SDK interfaces and assets. Full bundle bytes, uncompressed code payload, runtime download and installed runtime size are different measurements.
- Facts page: https://krate.tech/facts/

## Not to be confused with

Krate (krate.tech) is the Krate app runtime. It is not a Rust crate or crates.io package, and it is not related to krate.com, KrateSoft or the JavaScript project of the same name.

## Scoped benchmark

The following is the recorded 2026-08-25 notes comparison, not a measurement of the latest release or all Krate apps.
MarkText 0.17.1 ARM64 vs the Krate notes replica, Apple M4, macOS 27 (build 26A5388g), on AC power; equivalent-workload comparison, not feature parity.

- Historical app bundle versus installed application: Krate 36.6 KiB; MarkText 284.6 MiB installed.
- memory, 50,000-line document: Krate 178.5 MiB, one process; MarkText 2,299.4 MiB across four processes.
- warm start to a visible window, 50,000-line document: Krate 237.1 ms median; MarkText 611.5 ms median.

The historical Krate runtime was installed separately at 88.6 MiB. The 36.6 KiB app bundle is not the total first-install cost. Warm open is the median of ten runs per app; memory includes the whole process tree.

Energy was not measured. Source-bearing bundles can also include SDK interfaces and assets; the historical analysis does not establish the current full-bundle install ratio.

Analysis: https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/main/evidence/benchmarks/marktext-vs-krate/runs/20260825T085644Z/analysis.md
The public benchmark kit contains the protocol, analysis and seal. Retained raw run data is not all distributed in the public checkout.

# Answers about shipping desktop apps with Krate

## The .krate format: one app file for every screen

URL: https://krate.tech/portable-desktop-app-format.html
Reviewed: 2026-10-27 against Krate 0.5.4

A .krate is one small app file for every screen: the same bytes run natively on macOS, Windows and Linux, and sent as a link, it opens in any modern browser, phones included, with nothing to install and no account. The app starts with no access to your files or the network and asks before it touches either.

### One file, every screen

You build the app once and get one .krate file. Send it as a link and it opens in any modern browser, phones included, with nothing to install and no account. On Mac, Windows and Linux, the Krate runtime runs the same file natively, as a real window with no browser or WebView inside. The runtime is installed once and every Krate app after that is just a file.

There is no build per operating system, no build per processor and no package per platform to sign. Krate does the per-platform work in its runtimes, once, for every app. See how that compares with Electron and Tauri (https://krate.tech/desktop-app-distribution.html).

### Try one file tested on all three systems

Download chart.krate (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/incyashraj/krate/c46d29500f2b894c89285b04e1b5e2f75184e972/evidence/ported/chart.krate), a bar chart of a week's rainfall. Follow the sample instructions (https://krate.tech/docs/quickstart.html#try-the-chart-sample) to see what it asks for and run it. The Rust source (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/tree/c46d29500f2b894c89285b04e1b5e2f75184e972/apps/krate-chart) is available separately.

Full-file SHA-256: 3d290c48f74936d5cdb45ceb0ee945bd0f7b5b0b21f87f79917bced3b4ca73c3.

The same bundle passed headless replay and rendering checks on macOS, Windows and Linux in this CI run (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/actions/runs/35454102875) with source-built runtimes. Each host checks its own reference image:

- macOS: reference image (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/7701ad231e841c219f8493ad402b3ea0ff503af4/evidence/golden/macos-latest/chart.png) and recorded bundle hash (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/7701ad231e841c219f8493ad402b3ea0ff503af4/evidence/golden/macos-latest/chart.png.json).

- Windows: reference image (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/7701ad231e841c219f8493ad402b3ea0ff503af4/evidence/golden/windows-2022/chart.png) and recorded bundle hash (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/7701ad231e841c219f8493ad402b3ea0ff503af4/evidence/golden/windows-2022/chart.png.json).

- Linux: reference image (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/7701ad231e841c219f8493ad402b3ea0ff503af4/evidence/golden/ubuntu-latest/chart.png) and recorded bundle hash (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/7701ad231e841c219f8493ad402b3ea0ff503af4/evidence/golden/ubuntu-latest/chart.png.json).

### What is inside a .krate file?

The bundle is a ZIP-based application format. Its core entries are manifest.toml and code.wasm, and it can also carry assets, source and SDK material. Apps made in Studio carry their editable source, so you can keep changing them.

The manifest names the app and the access it asks for. The component calls Krate interfaces described in WIT, and the runtime supplies them. Files, the network and other host resources go through the capability model, so the app reaches only what the person allowed.

Read the bundle implementation (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/tree/main/crates/bundle) and interface definitions (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/tree/main/wit). Both are open source.

### Small by design

Krate's Notes app is one 36.6 KiB file. Holding 50,000 lines, it used 178.5 MiB of memory against 2,299.4 MiB for MarkText, an Electron editor: 13x less. A warm open took 237.1 ms against 611.5 ms: 2.6x faster. MarkText takes 284.6 MiB installed; the Krate runtime is installed once and shared by every app.

Measured on 25 August 2026 on an Apple M4: Krate's Notes app against MarkText 0.17.1 on the same 50,000-line notes workload, an equivalent workload. Read the method (https://krate.tech/reports/).

### Verify a shared file yourself

Copy the same file to each machine, record krate --version, see what it asks for and run it:

krate --version
krate run app.krate --dump-caps
krate run app.krate --prompt

Compare the full-file SHA-256 on each host: shasum -a 256 app.krate on macOS, sha256sum app.krate on Linux, Get-FileHash app.krate -Algorithm SHA256 in Windows PowerShell. Then use the app the same way on each: load data, save, close and reopen.

### Bring your project over

Krate is for real software, from small tools to editors, dashboards and games. Run krate port (beta) on an existing project to see how it maps to Krate's interfaces, or open it in Krate Studio and let the AI bring it over. Electron apps go from hundreds of megabytes to one small file. The porting guide (https://krate.tech/docs/porting.html) walks through it, and the capability reference (https://krate.tech/docs/limits.html) lists what apps can use today.

### Questions

Q: What does the person opening a .krate need?
A: Nothing, to open a link: the app runs in any modern browser, phones included, with no account. To run it natively, the Krate runtime, installed once. They never need Rust, your source or your build tools.

Q: Can a .krate file run on a phone?
A: Yes. Send it as a link and it opens in the phone's browser, with nothing to install and no account.

Q: Is a .krate the same as a Rust crate?
A: No. A crate is a Rust package on crates.io. A .krate file is a packaged application: a WebAssembly component, its manifest, and optional source and assets.

Q: How do I check that two copies are the same file?
A: Compare SHA-256 hashes: shasum -a 256 on macOS, sha256sum on Linux, Get-FileHash in Windows PowerShell. Matching hashes mean identical bytes.

## Share an app made with AI as one link

URL: https://krate.tech/share-an-app-made-with-ai.html
Reviewed: 2026-10-27 against Krate 0.5.4

Describe your app in Krate Studio, then send it as a link: it opens in any modern browser, phones included, with nothing to install and no account. On Mac, Windows and Linux the same .krate file also runs natively, and every app shows what it asks for before it opens.

### Make it by describing it

Open Krate Studio (https://krate.tech/studio/) on Mac, Windows or Linux, or in your browser (https://krate.tech/app/), and say what you want in plain words. The AI builds the app, checks it and packs it into one .krate. Then keep changing it by asking: a new button, a dark mode, a CSV export.

Desktop Studio works with Claude, Codex, Grok or Gemini. In the browser, Krate's own AI makes your first app. You do not need to know Rust; the AI writes it.

Developers can do the same from the command line with their own AI agent:

krate doctor
krate ai
krate create "a regex tester with a pattern box and live matches" --agent claude --output regex.krate

krate create --help lists every option.

### Test before you send it

Studio checks every build and opens the app for you to try. Click through it, resize the window, type a bad input. From the command line, see what it asks for and run it:

krate run regex.krate --dump-caps
krate run regex.krate --prompt

The first command shows the permission request without running anything. The second opens the app after you review it.

### Send it as a link or a file

As a link. Publish the app and you get a link like https://hub.krate.tech/run/<id>. Paste it into a chat or an email; it opens in any modern browser, phones included, with nothing to install and no account. Publishing needs a Krate account; opening never does.

krate publish regex.krate

As a file. Once you have tried the app, send the .krate itself by email, chat or a shared drive. One file, from 37 KB. On Mac, Windows and Linux, the Krate runtime opens it natively; here is what the person receiving it does (https://krate.tech/open/). They never need your AI account, your source or a Rust toolchain.

### What the person you send it to sees

Before the app opens, they see exactly what it asks for and decide. It starts with no access to their files or the network, hosts it did not declare stay unreachable, and it keeps its data in storage of its own. See how permissions work (https://krate.tech/run-ai-generated-code-safely.html) and how one file opens on every screen (https://krate.tech/portable-desktop-app-format.html).

### Questions

Q: Can I change the app after I send it?
A: Yes. Ask for the change, then send the new version. Studio keeps each version, so you can go back if a change goes wrong.

Q: Does the person I send it to need my AI tool or an account?
A: No. A link opens in their browser with nothing to install and no account. You need a Krate account only to publish a link; opening one never needs one.

Q: Which AI tools can make a .krate?
A: Krate Studio on your computer works with Claude, Codex, Grok or Gemini. In the browser, Krate's own AI makes your first app.

Q: Do I need to know how to code?
A: No. You describe the app in plain words and the AI writes the Rust, checks it and packs it. Developers can still open the source and change it by hand.

Q: Can I send it by email or chat?
A: Yes. A link or a .krate goes anywhere a picture goes: an email, a chat, a shared drive.

Q: What if my app needs the internet?
A: It declares each host it talks to, and the person opening it sees that list and approves it before the app runs. Hosts it did not declare stay unreachable.

## Run an AI-built app safely: see what it can touch first

URL: https://krate.tech/run-ai-generated-code-safely.html
Reviewed: 2026-10-27 against Krate 0.5.4

A Krate app starts with no access to your files or the network, and before it opens, from a link or from the file, you see exactly what it asks for and decide. An AI-built app reaches only what you allow: hosts it did not declare stay unreachable, and each app keeps its own storage.

### Read the permission request before it runs

Every Krate app lists what it wants in its manifest. You see that list before the app opens. From the command line you can read it without running anything:

krate run app.krate --dump-caps

Check the file scope, network hosts and devices against what the app is for. If a document viewer asks to upload data, you see it before a single line of it runs.

### Decide each grant when it opens

krate run app.krate --prompt

The runtime checks host operations against what you granted for that session. Refuse a capability the app requires and the app does not launch. Grant only what the task needs, and keep --auto-grant for apps you already know.

### Where enforcement happens

The app is a WebAssembly component. It has no direct line to your operating system: it calls Krate's WIT interfaces, and the native runtime implements them. Import validation and host-side capability checks enforce the boundary, and the permission dialog belongs to the runtime, not to the app.

Explore the interface definitions (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/tree/main/wit), the policy implementation (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/tree/main/crates/policy) and the architecture guide (https://krate.tech/docs/architecture.html). All of it is open source.

### A practical review checklist

- Get the app from someone you know, or check its publisher.
- Record its version and hash, and compare them with the ones the publisher shared.
- Read the permission request before it opens.
- Grant the narrowest access that does the job.
- Recheck the request when a new version arrives.

Found a problem in Krate itself? The project's security reporting policy (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/main/SECURITY.md) says how to report it.

### Questions

Q: Where does an app keep its data?
A: In storage of its own, kept per app, which it declares in its permission request. It gets no folder on your disk unless you grant one or pick a file for it.

Q: What can a Krate app do without asking?
A: Only harmless things: open its window, draw, play sound, read the clock and language settings, and show a dialog. Files, the network, the camera, the microphone and its own storage must be declared and approved.

Q: Is the permission screen enforced?
A: Yes. The runtime checks protected calls against what you allowed, and hosts the app did not declare stay unreachable. Grant only what the task needs.

Q: Can an app ask for more access while it runs?
A: No. Everything an app can reach is declared in its manifest and shown before it opens. A new need comes in a new version, and you see that request before the new version opens.

Q: Can I see what an app asks for without running it?
A: Yes. krate run app.krate --dump-caps prints the request without granting anything or starting the app.

Q: Does Krate replace my operating system's protections?
A: It adds to them. Your operating system still checks the Krate runtime itself; Krate then decides what each app inside it may touch.

## Krate vs Electron vs Tauri: what do you ship?

URL: https://krate.tech/desktop-app-distribution.html
Reviewed: 2026-10-27 against Krate 0.5.4

Electron and Tauri ship a separate package for each operating system; Krate ships one .krate file that runs natively on Mac, Windows and Linux and opens from a link in any browser, phones included. You build once, send once, and everyone gets the same file.

### One app, two shipping workflows

When you release an update, what has to reach each user? In the usual Electron or Tauri workflow, a separate build for their platform. With Krate, the same file for everyone.

Typical desktop packaging, compared with Krate. Read each row from build to delivery.

Electron / Tauri

- 1. DevelopShared application code

- 2. PackagePlatform-specific applications

- 3. DelivermacOS packageWindows packageLinux package

Krate

- 1. MakeDescribe it in Studio, or write it with the SDK

- 2. PackageOne app.krate file

- 3. DeliverA link for any browser, and the same file for Mac, Windows and Linux

A link opens the app in any modern browser with nothing to install. On a desktop, the Krate runtime runs the same file natively; it is installed once and shared by every Krate app.

See Electron's application packaging (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/application-distribution) and Tauri's distribution formats (https://tauri.app/distribute/). Electron's app.asar can package application source, but it is delivered inside a platform-specific Electron distribution; it is not a standalone cross-OS executable.

### Compare the distribution boundary

Desktop distribution models, reviewed 20 September 2026

Question | Electron | Tauri | Krate

Application artifact | Platform-specific packaged application. | Platform-specific application bundle or installer. | One .krate file for every system, and a link that opens it in any browser.

UI/runtime model | Chromium and Node.js in Electron's process model. | Web frontend in an OS WebView with a Rust backend. | WebAssembly app drawn natively by the Krate runtime, with no browser or WebView inside.

Recipient prerequisite | The packaged application and its platform requirements. | The packaged application and platform/WebView requirements. | Nothing, to open a link. The Krate runtime, installed once, to run it natively.

Existing app migration | Fits browser/Node-based applications. | Fits web UI with Rust/native integration. | krate port (beta) and Studio's AI bring the project over to Krate's APIs.

Electron's distribution guide (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/distribution-overview) covers packaging, signing, publishing and updates; its process model (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/process-model) explains Chromium and Node. Tauri documents platform-specific distribution (https://tauri.app/distribute/) and its WebView/Rust architecture (https://tauri.app/concept/architecture/). Tauri does not bundle Chromium like Electron.

### Can I send exactly the same file to all three systems?

Yes, with Krate. Build once and send the same .krate file to Mac, Windows and Linux users, or publish it and send one link. There is no separate application build per OS.

Try the downloadable Chart example (https://krate.tech/docs/quickstart.html#try-the-chart-sample). Its source, full-file checksum and three-OS test evidence (https://krate.tech/portable-desktop-app-format.html#try-one-file-tested-on-all-three-systems) let you check it yourself. No Rust toolchain or AI account is needed to run the file.

### Smaller, measured

Krate's Notes app is one 36.6 KiB file. Holding 50,000 lines, it used 178.5 MiB of memory against 2,299.4 MiB for MarkText, an Electron editor: 13x less. A warm open took 237.1 ms against 611.5 ms: 2.6x faster. MarkText takes 284.6 MiB installed; the Krate runtime is installed once and shared by every app.

Measured on 25 August 2026 on an Apple M4: Krate's Notes app against MarkText 0.17.1 on the same 50,000-line notes workload, an equivalent workload. Read the method (https://krate.tech/reports/).

### Bring your project over

Run krate port ./my-project (beta) to see how your app maps to Krate's interfaces, or open the project in Krate Studio and let the AI bring it over. Electron apps go from hundreds of megabytes to one small file. Start with one representative feature, then follow the porting checklist (https://krate.tech/docs/porting.html).

### What happens when the app changes?

Build the next .krate and publish it or send it. There is no app store in the way and no build per OS to redo. Runtime updates arrive separately, so your app stays one small file.

### Questions

Q: Which one should I pick?
A: Pick Krate when you want one file for every screen, a link anyone can open, and permissions the user approves. Electron and Tauri suit teams that want to keep a web codebase and ship a package per OS.

Q: What do users install with each?
A: With Electron and Tauri, each user installs your app's own package for their system. With Krate, nothing to open a link; to run it natively, the Krate runtime once, and then every .krate opens from the file.

Q: Can I send the same file to every system?
A: Yes, with Krate. Electron and Tauri produce a package per operating system; a .krate is the same bytes on macOS, Windows and Linux.

## How to distribute a desktop app: ship one file

URL: https://krate.tech/how-to-distribute-a-desktop-app.html
Reviewed: 2026-10-27 against Krate 0.5.4

Ship it as one .krate file: the same file runs natively on macOS, Windows and Linux, and sent as a link, it opens in any modern browser, phones included, with nothing to install and no account. There is no separate build, signature or download for each operating system, and the app asks before it touches anyone's files or the network.

### The usual route, step by step

- Build once per operating system. Electron and Tauri share your code, then produce a separate package for macOS, Windows and Linux. In practice that means a build machine or CI runner for each system, and macOS signing needs a Mac.

- Often build once per processor. Apple silicon and Intel Macs, x64 and ARM64 Windows, x86_64 and arm64 Linux each need native code built for them, or a universal build that carries both.

- Sign and notarize. For direct downloads, macOS expects a Developer ID signature and Apple notarization, which needs a paid Apple Developer Program membership. On Windows, an unsigned download shows "Windows protected your PC", and even a newly signed app can be flagged as unrecognized until it builds reputation.

- Package and host each one. A DMG or app bundle for macOS, an installer for Windows, and AppImage, deb, RPM, Flatpak or Snap for Linux. Each gets its own download link and its own update path.

After all that, a conventional desktop program usually runs with the same access to files and the network as the person who opened it, unless the platform sandboxes it, as the Mac App Store does. A signature says who made the app. It does not limit which of your files the app can read.

Sources: Electron's code signing guide (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/code-signing), Tauri's distribution guide (https://tauri.app/distribute/) and Microsoft's SmartScreen reputation guide (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/package-and-deploy/smartscreen-reputation).

### The Krate route

- Make the app. Describe it in Krate Studio (https://krate.tech/studio/) and the AI builds it, or write it in Rust with the Krate SDK. Studio can also bring over a project you already have.

- Pack one file. The result is one .krate, from 37 KB: a manifest that names the access the app wants, a WebAssembly component that holds the app, and optionally its assets and source. There is no machine code inside, so there is nothing to build per processor.

- Send it like a picture. Publish it and send the link, or email it, drop it in a chat or a shared folder. Everyone gets the same bytes.

- They open it anywhere. From a link, it opens in any modern browser, phones included, with nothing to install and no account. On Mac, Windows and Linux, the Krate runtime runs it natively; Krate for Mac is signed and notarized by Apple, and after the first install every new app is just its own file.

- They decide what it may touch. An app starts with no access to files or the network and asks for what it needs. The runtime checks protected calls against what was allowed. See how to see what an app asks for (https://krate.tech/run-ai-generated-code-safely.html).

### What you stop doing

You stop producing a separate package for each operating system and processor. You stop signing and notarizing each app for each platform, hosting a download per system, and asking people to run an installer that gets their full permissions. You ship one file, or one link, and spend the time on the app.

### Smaller, measured

Krate's Notes app is one 36.6 KiB file. Holding 50,000 lines, it used 178.5 MiB of memory against 2,299.4 MiB for MarkText, an Electron editor: 13x less. A warm open took 237.1 ms against 611.5 ms: 2.6x faster. MarkText takes 284.6 MiB installed; the Krate runtime is installed once and shared by every app.

Measured on 25 August 2026 on an Apple M4: Krate's Notes app against MarkText 0.17.1 on the same 50,000-line notes workload, an equivalent workload. Read the method (https://krate.tech/reports/).

### Check it yourself

Download chart.krate (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/incyashraj/krate/c46d29500f2b894c89285b04e1b5e2f75184e972/evidence/ported/chart.krate), one file of 11,455 bytes with SHA-256 3d290c48f74936d5cdb45ceb0ee945bd0f7b5b0b21f87f79917bced3b4ca73c3. Follow the quickstart (https://krate.tech/docs/quickstart.html#try-the-chart-sample) to see what it asks for and run it on any of the three systems.

Ten ported apps, as the same committed .krate files, passed their headless replay checks on macOS (Apple silicon), Ubuntu (x86_64) and Windows (x86_64) GitHub runners with runtime 0.5.4 on 29 September 2026. Records: macOS (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/59aeeebc8dafa5ec1700e01a44f8fe8fe7ab980e/evidence/e3/run-36557127592-replay-macos.tsv), Ubuntu (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/59aeeebc8dafa5ec1700e01a44f8fe8fe7ab980e/evidence/e3/run-36557127592-replay-ubuntu.tsv), Windows (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/59aeeebc8dafa5ec1700e01a44f8fe8fe7ab980e/evidence/e3/run-36557127592-replay-windows.tsv). Native runtimes are published for Apple silicon and Intel Macs, x64 and ARM64 Windows, and x86_64 and arm64 Linux.

### Questions

Q: Can one file run on Windows, macOS and Linux?
A: A normal native executable can't, because each system uses its own executable format. A .krate can: it holds a WebAssembly component that the Krate runtime runs natively on each system, and a link opens it in any browser too.

Q: Do the people I send it to need to install anything?
A: Not to open a link: it runs in their browser, phones included, with no account. To run it natively, they install the Krate runtime once from the download page (https://krate.tech/download/), and every Krate app after that is just a file.

Q: Do I need a code signing certificate to ship a .krate?
A: No. There is no package per operating system to sign and notarize, because a .krate isn't one. You can still sign a .krate with your own key so people can check it came from you; see code signing and Krate (https://krate.tech/desktop-app-code-signing.html).

Q: Can I ship an app I made with AI this way?
A: Yes. Make it in Krate Studio with the AI you already use, or bring an existing project into Studio. See how to share an app made with AI (https://krate.tech/share-an-app-made-with-ai.html).

## Krate vs Electron: one small native file with no browser inside

URL: https://krate.tech/krate-vs-electron.html
Reviewed: 2026-10-27 against Krate 0.5.4

Krate ships your app as one small .krate file that runs natively on Mac, Windows and Linux and opens from a link in any browser, phones included; Electron puts Chromium and Node.js inside every app and ships a package for each operating system. On the same 50,000-line notes workload, measured on 25 August 2026 on an Apple M4, Krate's Notes app used 13x less memory and opened 2.6x faster than MarkText 0.17.1, an Electron editor doing the equivalent work.

### Side by side

Electron and Krate, reviewed 6 October 2026 against Electron's official docs

Question | Electron | Krate

What you ship | A packaged app for each operating system, each carrying its own Chromium and Node.js. | One .krate file for every system, and a link that opens it in any browser.

App code | HTML, CSS and JavaScript in Chromium, with Node.js in the main process. | A WebAssembly component that calls Krate's interfaces. Describe it in Studio and the AI writes it, or write Rust yourself.

Builds per OS and CPU | One package per target platform. | One file. Krate builds the native runtimes.

Signing | Sign for Windows and macOS, and notarize for macOS, for each release. | No per-OS signing of the app file. Optional Krate signature with your own key.

Default access | Renderers are sandboxed by default since Electron 20. The main process is not sandboxed and has Node.js. | The app starts with no file or network access. The person running it grants or refuses each request.

Platforms | Windows, macOS and Linux. | macOS, Windows and Linux natively, and any modern browser from a link, phones included.

Electron facts: process model (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/process-model), process sandboxing (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/sandbox), code signing (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/code-signing) and distribution overview (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/distribution-overview).

### Measured against an Electron editor

Krate's Notes app is one 36.6 KiB file. Holding 50,000 lines, it used 178.5 MiB of memory against 2,299.4 MiB for MarkText, an Electron editor: 13x less. A warm open took 237.1 ms against 611.5 ms: 2.6x faster. MarkText takes 284.6 MiB installed; the Krate runtime is installed once and shared by every app.

Measured on 25 August 2026 on an Apple M4: Krate's Notes app against MarkText 0.17.1 on the same 50,000-line notes workload, an equivalent workload. Read the method (https://krate.tech/reports/).

### What one file changes for shipping

With Electron, each release is a set of platform builds that you sign, notarize and host. With Krate, each release is one new file. Send the link and it opens in any modern browser, phones included, with nothing to install and no account. On a desktop, the Krate runtime opens the file natively, and because every Krate app shares that runtime, a second or third app never brings another copy of a browser.

### Who decides what the app can touch

In Electron, the developer decides what the main process exposes to the sandboxed renderers, and the main process itself runs with the user's permissions. That is a sound design for code you wrote, but the person running the app has no say in it.

In Krate, the app lists what it wants in its manifest and the person running it approves or refuses, before it opens. The runtime checks protected calls against what was allowed, and hosts the app did not declare stay unreachable.

### Moving an Electron app to Krate

Start with a scan. It reads your source without building or running it and shows how each part maps to Krate:

krate port ./my-electron-app

krate port is in beta. Krate Studio can do the move with AI: it rewrites the app against the Krate SDK and shows its plan first. Electron apps go from hundreds of megabytes to one small file. Begin with one representative feature and read the porting guide (https://krate.tech/docs/porting.html).

### Questions

Q: How do I move an Electron app to Krate?
A: Run krate port (beta) on the project, or open it in Krate Studio: the AI rewrites it against Krate's interfaces and shows its plan first. The result is one small .krate file in place of a package per OS.

Q: Do Krate users need Chromium?
A: No. A Krate app runs natively, with no browser engine inside, and every Krate app shares one runtime. From a link, it opens in whatever browser the person already has.

Q: Do I need to know Rust?
A: No. Describe the app in Krate Studio and the AI writes the Rust for you. Developers who like Rust can write it by hand with the Krate SDK.

Q: Which one should I pick?
A: Pick Krate when you want one small file that opens anywhere, uses a fraction of the memory and asks before it touches anything. Electron suits a team with a large web codebase built on Node.js packages that wants to keep that code exactly as it is.

## Krate vs Tauri: one file for every desktop and every browser

URL: https://krate.tech/krate-vs-tauri.html
Reviewed: 2026-10-27 against Krate 0.5.4

Krate ships one .krate file with no WebView that runs natively on Mac, Windows and Linux and opens from a link in any browser, phones included; Tauri uses the system WebView and builds a separate bundle for each operating system. With Krate, the person running the app approves what it may touch before it opens.

### Side by side

Tauri and Krate, reviewed 6 October 2026 against Tauri's official docs

Question | Tauri | Krate

What you ship | An installer or bundle per platform: DMG or app bundle, a Windows installer, AppImage, deb, RPM, Flatpak or Snap. | One .krate file for macOS, Windows and Linux, and a link that opens it in any browser.

Interface | Your web frontend in the system WebView: WebView2, WKWebView or webkit2gtk. | Krate's own UI, drawn natively by the runtime. No WebView.

App logic | Rust commands, with plugins in Rust, Swift or Kotlin. | A WebAssembly component in Rust, written by you or by Studio's AI.

Permissions | Capability files the developer writes grant or deny commands per window. | The app requests access in its manifest; the person running it grants or refuses.

Signing | Required on most platforms. Direct macOS downloads also need notarization. | No per-OS signing of the app file. Optional Krate signature with your own key.

Platforms | Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS. | macOS, Windows and Linux natively, and any modern browser from a link, phones included.

Tauri facts: distribution (https://tauri.app/distribute/), capabilities (https://tauri.app/security/capabilities/) and WebView versions (https://tauri.app/reference/webview-versions/).

### Who holds the permissions

Tauri's capabilities limit what the frontend in the WebView may call. They are chosen by the developer, and Tauri's own docs (https://tauri.app/security/capabilities/) say they do not protect against malicious or insecure Rust code in the app itself. They protect users from a compromised frontend.

In Krate, the whole app is the guest. It has no direct line to the operating system; it calls Krate interfaces, and the runtime checks protected calls against what the person running it allowed.

### Shipping a release

With Tauri, a release means building on each platform, usually in a CI job per system, signing for each platform, and hosting and updating each package. With Krate, a release is one new .krate file. Publish it and send the link, and it opens in any modern browser, phones included, with nothing to install and no account; on a desktop, the same file runs natively.

### Moving a Tauri app to Krate

Both are Rust, so a lot comes with you. Run the scan, which reads your source without building it:

krate port ./my-tauri-app

krate port is in beta. Pure Rust logic often carries over as it is; the WebView interface moves to Krate's widgets, canvas and host interfaces, and Krate Studio's AI can do that part for you. See the porting guide (https://krate.tech/docs/porting.html).

### Questions

Q: Which one should a Rust developer pick?
A: Pick Krate when you want one file for every desktop and every browser, no WebView, and permissions the user approves before the app opens. Tauri suits a team that wants to keep a web frontend and ship a bundle per OS.

Q: What does the person I send it to install?
A: With Tauri, your app's own installer or bundle for their system. With Krate, nothing to open a link; to run it natively, the Krate runtime once, and then every .krate opens from the file.

Q: Is Krate built on Tauri?
A: No. Krate is its own runtime, built on Wasmtime. It does not use a WebView.

Q: How does a Tauri app move to Krate?
A: With a port. Rust logic often carries across, and krate port (beta) and Krate Studio's AI rewrite the WebView interface against Krate's interfaces.

Q: Which one makes smaller downloads?
A: Krate apps are tiny: Krate's Notes app is one 36.6 KiB file, and a link needs nothing installed. The native runtime is installed once and shared by every Krate app, so each new app is only its own file.

## Desktop app or web app? Ship one file that is both

URL: https://krate.tech/desktop-app-or-web-app.html
Reviewed: 2026-10-27 against Krate 0.5.4

With Krate you do not have to choose: a .krate opens from a link in any browser, phones included, like a web app, and runs natively on Mac, Windows and Linux like a desktop app. You run no server for either, and the app asks before it touches anyone's files or the network.

### Side by side

A hosted web app and a Krate app, reviewed 27 October 2026

Question | Hosted web app | Krate app

What people get | A page in a browser tab, or an installed web app where the browser supports it. | The app in their browser from a link, and a native window on Mac, Windows and Linux.

What you run | A server or hosting account, for as long as people use the app. | No server. Krate's hub serves the link, and the native app runs from the file.

Offline | Only with extra work, such as a service worker. | The native app works without a connection unless it needs the network itself.

Local files | Depends on the browser. The File System Access picker is not available in all major browsers (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/showOpenFilePicker). | Through a file dialog or a folder the person grants.

Updates | Every visitor gets the new version on reload. | You publish or send the new version.

Phones | Yes. | Yes, from a link in the phone's browser.

What people install | Nothing. | Nothing, to open a link. The Krate runtime, once, to run it natively.

### No server to run

A hosted app needs a domain, a hosting bill, uptime, sign-in and storage for user data, and it keeps people's data on your server, which brings privacy duties. A Krate app keeps its saved data on the person's computer, in storage of its own, unless they grant it network access. If it talks to a service, that service is yours to run; the app itself needs no hosting.

### Apps made with Lovable, Bolt, v0 and similar tools

These tools mostly produce web apps you have to host, or wrap per OS with Electron or Tauri. Krate gives you a better path: open the project in Krate Studio and the AI brings it over, rewriting it against Krate's interfaces and showing its plan first. You end up with one file that opens from a link and runs natively. Or skip the detour and describe the app to Studio from the start. See how to share an app made with AI (https://krate.tech/share-an-app-made-with-ai.html).

### Questions

Q: Does a Krate app need a server?
A: No. Krate's hub serves the link, and the native app runs on the person's computer from the file. If it calls an API you host, that service still runs, but the app itself needs no server and no domain.

Q: What does the person I send it to need?
A: Nothing, to open a link: it runs in their browser with no account. To run it natively, the Krate runtime, installed once for their system.

Q: Can I still use the web from a Krate app?
A: Yes. A Krate app can call APIs over HTTP and WebSockets for the hosts it declares, which the person approves before it runs.

Q: Can I turn my website into a desktop app?
A: Often, yes. krate port (beta) reads your project and shows what maps across, and Krate Studio's AI rewrites it against Krate's interfaces, so you get one file that runs natively and opens from a link, with no per-OS package to build or sign.

Q: Do Krate apps need an internet connection?
A: The native app does not, unless it uses the network itself, and then only to the hosts the person allows. A link needs a connection to load, like any page.

Q: Can people open a .krate on their phone?
A: Yes. Send a link and it opens in the phone's browser, with nothing to install and no account.

## Ship a desktop app without code signing for every OS

URL: https://krate.tech/desktop-app-code-signing.html
Reviewed: 2026-10-27 against Krate 0.5.4

A Krate app needs no code signing per operating system, because you send a link that opens in any browser or one .krate file that the Krate runtime opens natively. Native installers need an Apple Developer ID and notarization on macOS and a trusted signature on Windows; a Krate app skips that whole step.

### What signing takes for a native app

- macOS: an Apple Developer Program membership with an annual fee, Xcode on a Mac, signing certificates, then an upload to Apple for notarization.

- Windows: an unsigned download shows "Windows protected your PC" and the user must choose to run it anyway. A file signed with a new certificate can still be flagged as unrecognized until it builds reputation, and an EV certificate no longer skips that. On Windows 11, Smart App Control can block unsigned files that have no positive reputation.

- Linux: package and repository signing depends on the format and the store.

Sources: Electron's code signing guide (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/code-signing) and Microsoft's SmartScreen reputation guide (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/package-and-deploy/smartscreen-reputation).

### What a signature tells your users

A signature identifies the publisher and shows the file has not been changed since it was signed. It does not limit what the program can reach once it runs: a signed installer still gets the same access to files and the network as the person who opened it.

### How it works with Krate

From a link, it opens in any modern browser, phones included, with nothing to install and no account. There is no installer of yours for anyone to approve.

Natively, your app is a file the Krate runtime opens, not a program the operating system launches, so there is no per-OS package of yours to sign or notarize. Krate for Mac is signed and notarized by Apple. When someone opens your app, Krate shows what it asks for, and the app gets only what they allow.

### Signing a .krate with your own key

You can sign a bundle so recipients can check it came from you and has not changed. The key is an Ed25519 key you create; it stays on your machine, and signing and checking work offline with no account:

krate sign app.krate --key publisher.key --generate-key --namespace com.example.app

--generate-key writes a new key the first time and refuses to overwrite one. krate sign --help lists every option. Every release you sign is tied to your key.

### What you get back

- No Apple Developer Program fee and no notarization queue for your app.

- No certificate to buy, renew and keep safe for each platform.

- No reputation to build per release before people can open it.

- One file or one link per release, the same for everyone.

### Questions

Q: Does a Krate app need its own Apple Developer ID?
A: No. The app is a file that the Krate runtime opens, and Krate for Mac is signed and notarized by Apple. You do not sign or notarize the .krate for each system.

Q: Can I distribute a Windows app without a code signing certificate?
A: A native .exe without one shows a SmartScreen warning, and some managed or Smart App Control machines block it. With Krate there is no .exe of yours: you send a link that opens in the browser, or a .krate file the Krate runtime opens.

Q: Do I need an Apple Developer account to share a Mac app?
A: For a native Mac app downloaded from the web, in practice yes: notarization needs a Developer ID from the paid Apple Developer Program. A .krate is opened by Krate for Mac, which is signed and notarized, so you don't need your own Apple account to share one.

Q: Is a signed app safe to run?
A: A signature tells you who made it and that it was not changed. It does not limit what the app can do once it runs. Krate adds what a signature leaves out: the app asks before it gets your files or the network.

## Shipping a desktop app in 2026: questions and straight answers

URL: https://krate.tech/desktop-app-shipping-faq.html
Reviewed: 2026-10-27 against Krate 0.5.4

AI solved building the app, and Krate solves shipping it: one .krate file that runs natively on Mac, Windows and Linux and opens from a link in any browser, phones included. Each answer below starts with the answer, then links to the longer page.

### Questions

Q: How do I distribute a desktop app to Windows, macOS and Linux?
A: Ship one .krate file: it runs natively on all three, and a link opens it in any browser. The usual alternative is to build, sign and host a package for each system. Both routes, step by step (https://krate.tech/how-to-distribute-a-desktop-app.html).

Q: Can I ship one app file to Windows, Mac and Linux?
A: Yes, as a .krate: the same bytes run natively on all three, and the same app opens from a link in any browser. A normal native executable cannot do this. How the format works (https://krate.tech/portable-desktop-app-format.html).

Q: Can people open my app on their phone?
A: Yes. Send a link and it opens in the phone's browser, with nothing to install and no account. Sending an app as a link (https://krate.tech/share-an-app-made-with-ai.html).

Q: What is a good Electron alternative?
A: Krate, if you want one small file for every screen: it runs natively with no browser inside and opens from a link anywhere. Tauri, Wails and Neutralino keep a web frontend in the system WebView, and Flutter and Qt draw their own interface. Krate vs Electron (https://krate.tech/krate-vs-electron.html).

Q: Is there a Tauri alternative that doesn't need a build per OS?
A: Krate. Tauri builds an installer or bundle for each operating system; Krate ships one file and does the per-OS work once, in runtimes Krate maintains. Krate vs Tauri (https://krate.tech/krate-vs-tauri.html).

Q: How do I share an app I built with AI?
A: Make it in Krate Studio and send the link or the .krate file. If another AI tool built you a website, open the project in Krate Studio and bring it over. Sharing an app made with AI (https://krate.tech/share-an-app-made-with-ai.html).

Q: Can I ship a cross-platform app without code signing?
A: Yes, with Krate. You send a link or one .krate file, so there is no package per OS to sign, while native installers effectively need signing on macOS and Windows. Code signing and Krate (https://krate.tech/desktop-app-code-signing.html).

Q: How can I run an untrusted desktop app more safely?
A: For an unknown native program, use the strongest isolation you have, such as a virtual machine or Windows Sandbox. A Krate app starts with no file or network access and shows what it asks for before it opens; krate run app.krate --dump-caps prints the request without running it. Seeing what an app asks for (https://krate.tech/run-ai-generated-code-safely.html).

Q: Is there a portable app format that runs on every OS?
A: Yes: a .krate runs natively on macOS, Windows and Linux and opens from a link in any modern browser, phones included. AppImage is Linux only, Cosmopolitan's Actually Portable Executable runs one executable on several systems, mainly for command-line programs, and Java apps need a Java runtime. The .krate format (https://krate.tech/portable-desktop-app-format.html).

Q: Is there a WebAssembly runtime for desktop GUI apps?
A: Yes. Krate runs desktop apps compiled to WebAssembly components, with windows, widgets, a 2D canvas, files, storage and networking behind permissions. It embeds Wasmtime, while general runtimes such as Wasmtime, Wasmer and WasmEdge focus on servers and command-line programs. Krate's architecture (https://krate.tech/docs/architecture.html).

Q: Do people need to install anything to open a .krate?
A: No, not to open a link: it runs in any modern browser with no account. To run apps natively, they install Krate (https://krate.tech/download/) once; read what to do when someone sends you a .krate (https://krate.tech/open/).

Q: Is Krate free and open source?
A: Yes. The runtime, the .krate format and the CLI are open source under MIT OR Apache-2.0, and Krate Studio is under the Business Source License 1.1. Licence details (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate#license).

Q: Can I bring an existing app to Krate?
A: Yes. krate port (beta) brings a project over, and Krate Studio can do it with AI. Electron apps go from hundreds of megabytes to one small file; the porting guide (https://krate.tech/docs/porting.html) shows how.

## Electron alternatives in 2026, compared by what you ship

URL: https://krate.tech/electron-alternatives.html
Reviewed: 2026-10-27 against Krate 0.5.4

The main Electron alternatives are Tauri, Wails, Neutralinojs, Flutter, Qt and Krate, and the biggest difference is what you hand to people: Krate ships one .krate file that runs natively on every desktop and opens from a link in any browser, while the others ship a build for each operating system. A Krate app starts with no file or network access until the person allows it.

### The short list

Electron and its alternatives, from each project's official docs, read 6 October 2026

Tool | What you ship | How it draws the UI | App languages | Phones

Electron | A package per operating system, each with its own Chromium and Node.js. | Its own Chromium. | JavaScript, HTML, CSS. | No.

Tauri | A bundle or installer per operating system, plus store packages for mobile. | The system WebView. | A web frontend, with Rust in the core. | Yes.

Wails | A binary per operating system and architecture, with an optional Windows installer. | The system WebView. | Go, with a web frontend. | Only in v3, marked experimental.

Neutralinojs | A prebuilt binary per operating system and CPU, all made by one build on any host, plus a resources file. | The system WebView. | JavaScript, HTML, CSS. | No.

Flutter | A build per operating system (.exe with DLLs, .app, or a Linux package). | Its own widgets and renderer, no WebView. | Dart. | Yes.

Qt | A per-platform build, static or with Qt's shared libraries. | Its own widgets or scene graph, no WebView by default. | C++, QML, or Python through Qt for Python. | Yes.

Krate | One .krate file for every desktop, and a link that opens it in any browser. | The Krate runtime draws a native window, with no browser or WebView. | Describe it and Studio's AI writes it, or write Rust. | Yes, from a link in the phone's browser.

Sources: Electron (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/) and Electron Forge (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/forge-overview), Tauri distribution (https://tauri.app/distribute/) and Tauri webviews (https://tauri.app/reference/webview-versions/), Wails (https://wails.io/docs/introduction), Neutralinojs (https://neutralino.js.org/docs/) and its distribution overview (https://neutralino.js.org/docs/distribution/overview/), Flutter desktop (https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/desktop) and supported platforms (https://docs.flutter.dev/reference/supported-platforms), Qt deployment (https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/deployment.html) and supported platforms (https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/supported-platforms.html).

### What the user installs, and what the app can touch

Install and access, from each project's official docs, read 6 October 2026

Tool | What the user installs | What limits the app

Electron | Your app's own package. | Renderers run in Chromium's sandbox by default since Electron 20; the main process is not sandboxed.

Tauri | Your app's own package; on Windows it relies on WebView2, which the installer can add on older systems. | Capabilities limit what the frontend can call; the Rust core has full access to system resources.

Wails | Your app's own binary; on Windows the WebView2 runtime is needed. | The v2 guides linked here describe Go methods bound to the frontend, not a permission model.

Neutralinojs | Your app's own binary and resources file. | An allow list and a block list in the config control which native APIs the frontend can call.

Flutter | Your app's own package; on Windows, the Visual C++ redistributables too. | macOS builds use App Sandbox by default, with entitlements for network, camera or files.

Qt | Your app, plus Qt's libraries unless the system already has them. | Permission APIs ask for operating-system consent, such as the microphone; no Qt-level sandbox is described.

Krate | Nothing, to open a link. The Krate runtime, once, to run apps natively; then every .krate opens from its file. | The whole app starts with no file or network access; the person sees what it asks for and grants it before it opens.

Sources: Electron sandbox (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/sandbox), Tauri security (https://v2.tauri.app/security/) and capabilities (https://tauri.app/security/capabilities/), Wails on Windows (https://wails.io/docs/guides/windows), Neutralinojs configuration (https://neutralino.js.org/docs/configuration/neutralino.config.json/), Flutter on macOS (https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/macos/building), Qt permissions (https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/permissions.html).

### How to choose

- You want one file for every screen, with permissions the user approves: Krate. It is the only option here where the same file runs natively on macOS, Windows and Linux and opens from a link in any browser.

- You have a web app and want it on the desktop as it is: Electron, or Tauri, Wails or Neutralinojs if you want the system WebView instead of a bundled Chromium.

- You want store apps for phones: Flutter, Qt or Tauri. For phones without a store, a Krate link opens in the phone's browser.

- You write C++ or need a long-established widget toolkit: Qt.

Every native installer needs signing on macOS and Windows; the code signing page (https://krate.tech/desktop-app-code-signing.html) explains what that takes, and the distribution guide (https://krate.tech/how-to-distribute-a-desktop-app.html) walks through both routes.

### Measured against an Electron editor

Krate's Notes app is one 36.6 KiB file. Holding 50,000 lines, it used 178.5 MiB of memory against 2,299.4 MiB for MarkText, an Electron editor: 13x less. A warm open took 237.1 ms against 611.5 ms: 2.6x faster. MarkText takes 284.6 MiB installed; the Krate runtime is installed once and shared by every app.

Measured on 25 August 2026 on an Apple M4: Krate's Notes app against MarkText 0.17.1 on the same 50,000-line notes workload, an equivalent workload. Read the method (https://krate.tech/reports/).

### Try Krate in five minutes

Download Krate (https://krate.tech/download/), then open chart.krate (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/incyashraj/krate/c46d29500f2b894c89285b04e1b5e2f75184e972/evidence/ported/chart.krate), an 11,455-byte chart app, on any of the three systems. The quickstart (https://krate.tech/docs/quickstart.html) shows how to see what it asks for before it runs. Or describe your own app in Krate Studio (https://krate.tech/studio/).

### Questions

Q: Which Electron alternatives use the system WebView?
A: Tauri, Wails and Neutralinojs. Flutter and Qt draw their own interface, and Krate's runtime draws a native window with no browser or WebView.

Q: Can I keep my web frontend?
A: Tauri, Wails and Neutralinojs keep it in a WebView. Krate brings the app over instead: krate port (beta) and Studio's AI rewrite it as one small native file with no browser inside.

Q: Which alternative ships one file for every operating system?
A: Krate. Neutralinojs builds every platform's binary in one step, but you still ship one binary per system; a .krate is the same file on macOS, Windows and Linux, and a link opens it in any browser.

Q: Do any of them sandbox apps by default?
A: Electron sandboxes renderers by default; Tauri limits what the frontend can call; Flutter's macOS builds use App Sandbox. In Krate the whole app starts with no file or network access until the person allows it.

## Tauri alternatives in 2026, compared by what you ship

URL: https://krate.tech/tauri-alternatives.html
Reviewed: 2026-10-27 against Krate 0.5.4

If you like Tauri's small apps but want to stop building, signing and hosting a bundle for each operating system, Krate ships one .krate file that runs natively on every desktop and opens from a link in any browser, phones included. Electron, Wails and Flutter are the other common choices, each with a build per OS.

### Why people look past Tauri

Tauri is a good tool, and its apps are small because they use the system WebView. Three things send people looking anyway, all from Tauri's own docs:

- A build per system. Tauri ships an app bundle and DMG on macOS, MSI or NSIS installers on Windows, and Linux packages, each built for that platform (distribution (https://tauri.app/distribute/)).

- A different WebView on each system. WebView2 on Windows, WKWebView on macOS and webkit2gtk on Linux, so the same frontend renders through three engines (webview versions (https://tauri.app/reference/webview-versions/)).

- Permissions cover the frontend, not the core. Capabilities limit what the WebView can call; code in the Rust core and plugins has full access to system resources (security (https://v2.tauri.app/security/)).

### Side by side

Tauri and its alternatives, from each project's official docs, read 6 October 2026

Tool | What you ship | Rendering | What limits the app | Phones

Tauri | A bundle or installer per operating system. | The system WebView. | Capabilities for the frontend; the Rust core is unconstrained. | Yes.

Krate | One .krate file for every desktop, and a link for any browser. | The Krate runtime draws a native window; no WebView. | The whole app starts with no file or network access until the person allows it. | Yes, from a link in the phone's browser.

Electron | A package per operating system with its own Chromium and Node.js. | Bundled Chromium. | Renderers sandboxed by default; the main process is not. | No.

Wails | A binary per operating system and architecture. | The system WebView. | Go methods bound to the frontend. | v3 only, experimental.

Flutter | A build per operating system. | Its own renderer; no WebView. | App Sandbox by default on macOS builds. | Yes.

Sources: Tauri (https://v2.tauri.app/start/), Electron sandbox (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/sandbox), Wails cross-platform builds (https://wails.io/docs/guides/crossplatform-build), Flutter architecture (https://docs.flutter.dev/resources/architectural-overview) and Flutter on macOS (https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/macos/building).

### Krate for Tauri developers

Both are Rust. What changes is where the app runs and what you hand people. A Krate app is a WebAssembly component that calls Krate's interfaces for its window, drawing, files, network and storage. The Krate runtime runs the same file natively on every desktop and checks protected calls against what the person granted, and a link opens the same app in any browser.

There is no WebView, so the interface is written against Krate's interfaces, by hand or by Krate Studio's AI. Rust logic that builds for WebAssembly comes with you. Start with a scan that reads your project without building or running it:

krate port ./my-tauri-app

It lists what maps cleanly and what needs a permission. krate port is in beta, and the porting guide (https://krate.tech/docs/porting.html) covers the rest.

### Questions

Q: Can I reuse my Tauri Rust code in Krate?
A: Yes, logic that builds for WebAssembly usually carries over. Calls into the operating system and the WebView interface move to Krate's interfaces, and krate port (beta) reports what each part takes.

Q: Does Krate use a WebView?
A: No. The Krate runtime draws the app's window itself, so your app does not render through three different browser engines.

Q: Do the Tauri alternatives support phones?
A: Flutter does, and Wails v3 has experimental mobile support; Electron does not. Krate opens the same file from a link in any phone browser, with nothing to install.

Q: What do people install to open a Krate app?
A: Nothing, to open a link. To run apps natively, the Krate runtime, once for their system; after that every .krate opens from the file and shows what it asks for first.

## Cross-platform desktop app frameworks in 2026, compared by what you ship

URL: https://krate.tech/cross-platform-desktop-app-frameworks.html
Reviewed: 2026-10-27 against Krate 0.5.4

Krate is the framework that ships one file for every screen: the same .krate runs natively on Mac, Windows and Linux and opens from a link in any browser, phones included. Electron, Tauri, Flutter and Qt each ship a build per operating system, and the table below shows how they compare.

### The comparison

Five frameworks, from each project's official docs, read 6 October 2026

Question | Electron | Tauri | Flutter | Qt | Krate

What you ship | A package per OS | A bundle per OS | A build per OS | A build per platform | One .krate file, and a link

What the user installs | Your package | Your package; WebView2 on older Windows | Your package; VC++ redistributables on Windows | Your app with Qt's libraries | Nothing for a link; the Krate runtime, once, to run natively

Per-OS builds | Yes; some installers only build on their own OS | Yes; macOS bundles on a Mac, MSI on Windows | Yes, with each OS's toolchain | Yes, each platform's environment | No; one build

Signing | Sign and notarize per OS | Sign and notarize per OS | Notarize on macOS; signed MSIX on Windows | macdeployqt can sign for notarization | None per OS for the app file

Sandbox and permissions | Renderers sandboxed; main process not | Capabilities for the frontend; core unconstrained | App Sandbox on macOS builds | OS consent APIs; no Qt sandbox | Whole app starts with no file or network access

App languages | JavaScript, HTML, CSS | Web frontend, Rust core | Dart | C++, QML, Python | Rust, or described in plain words to Studio's AI

Phones | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, from a link in the browser

Current release | Latest three majors supported | Stable v2; v3 in alpha | Stable, 3.47 | Qt 6.12, September 2026 | 0.5.4, September 2026

Sources: Electron distribution (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/distribution-overview), signing (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/code-signing) and sandbox (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/sandbox); Tauri distribution (https://tauri.app/distribute/), security (https://v2.tauri.app/security/) and webviews (https://tauri.app/reference/webview-versions/); Flutter desktop (https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/desktop), macOS builds (https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/macos/building) and platforms (https://docs.flutter.dev/reference/supported-platforms); Qt deployment (https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/deployment.html), permissions (https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/permissions.html) and platforms (https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/supported-platforms.html). Wails and Neutralinojs are on the Electron alternatives (https://krate.tech/electron-alternatives.html) page.

### Three questions that decide it

- Do you want to hand people one file for every screen? Then Krate. Every other option here produces a separate build for each operating system.

- Do you need phones? Flutter, Qt and Tauri build store apps. A Krate app opens on a phone from a link, with no store and nothing to install.

- Do you have a web codebase you want to keep as it is? Then Electron or Tauri. Flutter, Qt and Krate each draw their own interface, and Krate Studio's AI can rewrite yours.

A fourth question sits under all of them: who decides what the app may touch? In most frameworks the developer decides. In Krate the person running the app sees what it asks for and grants it, and the runtime enforces that.

### Signing and installers, whichever you pick

A native installer is signed for each system. On macOS, software distributed with a Developer ID must be notarized by Apple (Apple (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/notarizing-macos-software-before-distribution)). On Windows, unsigned apps show a SmartScreen warning, and new signed apps can still warn until they build reputation (Microsoft (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/package-and-deploy/smartscreen-reputation)).

A .krate file is not a native installer, so there is no per-OS signing of the app, and a link needs no install at all. On macOS the Krate runtime is signed and notarized by Apple. More on the code signing page (https://krate.tech/desktop-app-code-signing.html).

### One file, proven on three systems

The same .krate files pass automated checks on macOS, Windows and Linux in CI: 10 apps on all three at Krate 0.5.4.

Ten ported apps, as the same committed .krate files, passed their headless replay checks on macOS (Apple silicon), Ubuntu (x86_64) and Windows (x86_64) GitHub runners with runtime 0.5.4 on 29 September 2026. Records: macOS (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/59aeeebc8dafa5ec1700e01a44f8fe8fe7ab980e/evidence/e3/run-36557127592-replay-macos.tsv), Ubuntu (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/59aeeebc8dafa5ec1700e01a44f8fe8fe7ab980e/evidence/e3/run-36557127592-replay-ubuntu.tsv), Windows (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate/blob/59aeeebc8dafa5ec1700e01a44f8fe8fe7ab980e/evidence/e3/run-36557127592-replay-windows.tsv). Native runtimes are published for Apple silicon and Intel Macs, x64 and ARM64 Windows, and x86_64 and arm64 Linux.

### Measured against an Electron editor

Krate's Notes app is one 36.6 KiB file. Holding 50,000 lines, it used 178.5 MiB of memory against 2,299.4 MiB for MarkText, an Electron editor: 13x less. A warm open took 237.1 ms against 611.5 ms: 2.6x faster. MarkText takes 284.6 MiB installed; the Krate runtime is installed once and shared by every app.

Measured on 25 August 2026 on an Apple M4: Krate's Notes app against MarkText 0.17.1 on the same 50,000-line notes workload, an equivalent workload. Read the method (https://krate.tech/reports/).

### Questions

Q: What is the best cross-platform desktop app framework?
A: For one file on every screen, Krate: it runs natively on every desktop and opens from a link in any browser. For an existing web codebase, Electron or Tauri; for store apps on phones, Flutter, Qt or Tauri.

Q: Which framework needs no build per operating system?
A: Krate: you build one .krate file and the runtime on each system opens it. The others produce a build for each operating system.

Q: Which frameworks avoid a browser engine?
A: Flutter and Qt draw their own interface, and so does Krate's runtime. Electron bundles Chromium, and Tauri uses the system WebView.

Q: Is Krate open source?
A: Yes. The runtime, the .krate format and the CLI are MIT OR Apache-2.0, and Krate Studio is under the Business Source License 1.1. The source is on GitHub (https://github.com/incyashraj/krate).
